newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Enron loses in N Sea gas transport case.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Enron loses in N Sea gas transport case.

text.p: The judgement in the British High Court on Tuesday in favour of pipeline group CATS (Central Area Transmission System) in its dispute with a subsidiary of Enron is not necessarily the end of the story.
Enron Corp chairman and CEO Kenneth Lay has already said the company may appeal the decision.
"While we respect the decision of the court, we continue to believe in the merits of our case, and we will carefully consider our options to appeal," he said.

The dispute revolved around use of the 255 mile long CATS pipeline under a Capacity Reservation and Transportation Agreement (CRTA) between Teesside Gas Transportation Limited, an Enron subsidiary, and the CATS owners.

The agreement was for the transport of gas from the North Sea's J-Block to Teesside. And Enron has also been involved in a lengthy dispute with the J-Block owners over its contractual purchase of gas from there, as well as with the pipeline owners.

In the CATS case, TGTL contracted to book space in CATS from April 1993 under a "send or pay" deal. This means the capacity holder is required to pay for the space on the pipeline regardless of whether it uses it.

TGTL continued to pay for capacity until the end of 1994, when it stopped on the grounds that the CATS owners had failed to comply with the CRTA and so the contract had terminated and no payment was due.
CATS sued in March 1995 to recover the money, and Enron counterclaimed by arguing that CATS was unable to provide the services contracted for.
The High Court found that TGTL was not entitled to terminate the CRTA, and also dismissed the counterclaim. It ruled that Enron had to repay the payment and interest since TGTL stopped paying.

Amoco, as operator of CATS, said in a statement that the amount involved is "in excess of 150 million stg," a view endorsed by BG plc which has interests of 51.18 percent in CATS through two subsidiaries.

Enron argues that the amount is much less, saying in a statement that "TGTL is required to release withheld send or pay payments to the CATS parties in the amount of approximately 70 million stg plus interest and costs."

The difference is explained as the Amoco figure includes all payments due since the contract started in April 1993, while Enron was only considering the payments that have been withheld until December 1996. A full decision on the amount due is expected in court on Wednesday.

The background of the case is closely bound up with Enron's contract with the J-Block producers to buy gas under a take or pay contract from the block. The level of send or pay payments to CATS, and of take or pay payments to J-Block's owners were fixed in 1990 and 1993 respectively, subject to indexation only.

The High Court pointed out that the combined cost of the gas and its transport came to 19 pence a therm, when the spot gas price was around 22 pence a therm, "providing a sound commercial basis for the Agreements when they were made." But by the spring and summer of 1995, the spot price fell to below 10 pence, "thereby making the Agreements ones in respect of which very substantial losses could be expected by the purchasers."

The judge found that Enron's principal motivation, at least from February 1995, was "the enormous losses they faced...the Plaintiffs were justified in their growing belief that that was so and that any and every point or opportunity would be seized upon by the Defendants if they thought it could or might provide them with a chance of escaping from or negotiating out of their commercial dilemma."

He added that "but for the fall in gas prices all of the matters of which the Defendants complain could and would have been readily sorted out in the spirit of co-operation which existed before then."
On Monday, Enron announced that it had settled its dispute with the J-Block owners. Enron is to pay $440 million, and in turn the take or pay contract has been renegotiated at a lower price.

A spokeswoman for Enron pointed out on Tuesday that the second quarter charge to income announced by Enron on Monday in respect of the J-Block settlement "fully reflects transportation issues as well as producer contract issues."

She added that this meant Enron had already factored in the likely cost of losing the CATS case in its provision for the J-Block case, although she added that Enron was not aware of the decision ahead of Tuesday's judgment in court.

Clive Fowler, Managing Director of Amoco (UK) Exploration Company, the operator of CATS, said on Tuesday he was delighted with the judgment. "It is a vindication of our decision to initiate legal action following Enron's refusal to make payments due. It is also a vindication of the integrity of the CATS system."
He said that the case had not been detrimental to the reputation or image of CATS, saying "we are continuing to sign up customers and are actively looking to expand."
"We think CATS is a great North Sea success story. We're looking forward to continued success in the future and to putting this litigation behind us," he said.
